To replace all PPE with warning signs
To discipline employees after an incident

options.text: All of the above — dust, fumes, and vapors

questions.questionText: An employee reports headaches when using a solvent in a small, poorly ventilated room. What should happen first?

options.text: Tell the employee to take a break and then continue the task
Report the concern and evaluate the task, chemical, ventilation, and controls before resuming normal work
Increase the solvent quantity to complete the task faster

questions.oshaClause: OSHA Industrial Hygiene / General Duty Clause

questions.questionText: Which type of control is generally preferred before relying on PPE?

options.text: Ignoring the exposure if the task is short

Which routes can chemicals use to enter the body?

options.text: All of the above — inhalation, skin absorption, and ingestion

options.text: Continue working since a dust collector is present
Move further from the dust source and continue the task
Report the problem immediately so it can be inspected, repaired, and verified before exposure continues

questions.questionText: PPE must be properly selected, fitted, worn, maintained, and replaced when necessary.
Which of the following is an example of an ergonomic hazard?

options.text: All of the above — repetitive motion, awkward posture, and heavy lifting

questions.questionText: A job task produces high noise levels and employees report ringing in their ears after each shift. What type of hazard is present?
Employees should report symptoms and near misses even when no formal injury has occurred.

options.text: To assign blame for past incidents
To identify jobs, tasks, materials, and areas that may create health hazards
To create production and staffing schedules
To document employee attendance and overtime

industrial-hygiene-overview.title: What Industrial Hygiene Means
industrial-hygiene-overview.content: Industrial hygiene is the practice of anticipating, recognizing, evaluating, and controlling workplace conditions that can cause illness, discomfort, or long-term health problems. Unlike obvious injuries, industrial hygiene focuses on exposures that may build up over time — vapors, dusts, fumes, noise, heat, vibration, biological agents, or poorly designed tasks. A worker may not notice solvent vapors right away, but repeated exposure can cause irritation, dizziness, or long-term health effects. A noisy machine may seem routine, but daily exposure can lead to hearing loss. OSHA describes industrial hygienists as professionals who use monitoring, analysis, and controls to detect and reduce worker exposure. Industrial hygiene is not limited to chemical hazards — it covers biological, physical, and ergonomic hazards as well.

worksite-analysis.title: Worksite Analysis — Finding the Source of Exposure
worksite-analysis.content: A worksite analysis identifies jobs, tasks, equipment, and work areas that may create health hazards. A thorough analysis examines all operations and work activities, looking at what materials are used, how tasks are performed, how often employees are exposed, and what controls are already in place. Sanding creates dust. Welding creates fumes. Cleaning creates vapors. A poorly ventilated room allows contaminants to build up. Worksite analysis is an essential first step for determining exposure sources, problem tasks, and risks before controls can be selected or implemented. Employees often notice symptoms, odors, visible dust, or equipment problems before anyone else, making their input a critical part of any analysis.

air-contaminants.title: Air Contaminants and Chemical Hazards
air-contaminants.content: Air contaminants include dusts, fumes, mists, aerosols, fibers, gases, and vapors. Chemical hazards can enter the body through inhalation — the most common route — skin absorption, or ingestion. Exposure risk depends on the toxicity of the substance, the level of exposure, and the duration of exposure. Warning signs of air contamination include detectable odors, visible dust or mist in the air, skin or eye irritation, dizziness, and residue on work surfaces. Safety Data Sheets (SDS) describe the hazards, exposure limits, and required controls for each chemical. Controls include ventilation, substitution with less hazardous materials, closed containers, safe handling procedures, and appropriate PPE such as respirators and gloves.

biological-physical-ergonomic.title: Biological, Physical, and Ergonomic Hazards
biological-physical-ergonomic.content: Industrial hygiene covers hazard categories beyond chemicals. Biological hazards include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other organisms that can cause illness — healthcare workers, sanitation workers, and laboratory personnel are commonly exposed. Physical hazards include noise, vibration, radiation, temperature extremes (heat stress and cold stress), and lighting problems — ringing in the ears after a noisy shift is an early sign of noise-induced hearing damage. Ergonomic hazards include repetitive motion, awkward posture, forceful exertion, poor tool design, and heavy lifting — common in warehousing, manufacturing, and healthcare. Anything in the work environment that can affect employee health belongs in the industrial hygiene conversation.

evaluating-exposure.title: Evaluating Exposure and Recognizing Warning Signs
evaluating-exposure.content: Exposure evaluation may include observation, employee interviews, air sampling, noise monitoring, ventilation checks, review of SDS information, review of injury and illness records, and trend analysis. Employees play a key role because they often detect warning signs before anyone else: unusual odors, visible dust, skin or eye irritation, headaches, dizziness, ringing in the ears, or failed ventilation equipment. Reporting a concern is not complaining — it is part of prevention. The sooner a hazard is identified, the sooner it can be evaluated and controlled. When employees notice symptoms or equipment problems, they should report them immediately so the task, chemical, ventilation, exposure duration, and existing controls can all be reviewed before work resumes as normal.

hazard-controls.title: Controlling Workplace Health Hazards
hazard-controls.content: OSHA uses a hierarchy of controls that favors eliminating or substituting the hazard before relying on administrative controls or PPE. Engineering controls reduce or remove the hazard at its source — local exhaust ventilation to capture fumes, enclosures around noise sources, or substituting a hazardous chemical with a less hazardous alternative. Work practice controls change how work is performed — keeping containers closed, washing hands before eating, or using wet methods to suppress dust. Administrative controls change schedules, staffing, or task duration to reduce exposure time — job rotation is one example. PPE — respirators, gloves, goggles, hearing protection, and protective clothing — protects the worker when other controls are not yet sufficient, but it should never be the only line of defense. A control that fails (blocked exhaust, damaged PPE) must be reported and repaired immediately.

employee-participation.title: Employee Participation and Continuous Improvement
employee-participation.content: Industrial hygiene works best when employees, supervisors, and safety professionals all take part. Employees should follow written procedures and safe work practices, use ventilation, enclosures, and other controls as intended, wear required PPE correctly, and report damaged or missing equipment. Employees should read SDS before using hazardous materials, keep food, drinks, tobacco, and cosmetics out of contaminated areas, and participate honestly in exposure evaluations and training. Employees should report symptoms, odors, leaks, spills, equipment problems, and near misses — even when no formal injury has occurred. Reporting early means hazards can be found, evaluated, and corrected before someone becomes seriously ill. Workers often understand what creates hazards and whether controls are actually working in practice.

1.questionText: Industrial hygiene as a workplace discipline is best described as:

options.text: A method for investigating injuries after they occur
The practice of anticipating, recognizing, evaluating, and controlling workplace health hazards
A program that replaces all PPE with engineering controls
A system for disciplining employees who violate safety rules

4.questionText: An employee begins experiencing headaches shortly after starting a solvent task in a poorly ventilated area. What is the correct initial response?

options.text: Have the employee work faster to reduce total exposure time
Provide a dust mask and instruct the employee to continue
Stop the task, report the concern, and evaluate the exposure before resuming work
Open a nearby window and continue without further evaluation

4.oshaClause: OSHA Industrial Hygiene / General Duty Clause

5.questionText: According to the hierarchy of controls, which approach is preferred over relying on PPE for protecting workers?

options.text: Administrative controls such as posting warning signs
Verbal reminders from supervisors before each task
Engineering controls that eliminate or reduce the hazard at its source

6.questionText: A work practice control addresses workplace health hazards by changing the way a task is performed.

7.questionText: Skin contact with a hazardous chemical is an example of which route of entry?

8.questionText: Workers notice dust escaping from a loose connection in an exhaust ventilation system. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Continue working because the ventilation system is present
Move workstations further away from the exhaust connection
Report the deficiency so the system can be inspected and repaired before exposure continues
Continue work as long as the visible dust appears minimal

9.questionText: An employee may share a respirator with a coworker as long as it is cleaned between each use.

10.questionText: Which of the following correctly identifies ergonomic risk factors?

options.text: Bacterial contamination of a work surface
Prolonged exposure to high noise levels
Repetitive motion, awkward posture, and heavy lifting
Solvent vapors exceeding permissible exposure limits

11.questionText: Employees operating loud machinery report ringing in their ears at the end of each shift. This symptom is most consistent with which type of workplace hazard?

options.text: A physical hazard — occupational noise exposure
An ergonomic hazard from repetitive motion

12.questionText: Employees should only report health concerns when a formal recordable injury has already been documented.

13.questionText: Before selecting hazard controls, what must an employer first do?

options.text: Assign blame for past incidents to specific employees
Identify and analyze the jobs, tasks, and materials that may create employee health hazards
Purchase and distribute PPE to all employees
Post OSHA hazard communication posters in break rooms

14.questionText: Replacing a highly toxic solvent with a less hazardous cleaning agent is an example of which type of control?

15.questionText: Bacteria, viruses, and fungi encountered in the workplace are classified as biological hazards in industrial hygiene.
